pages.x: By the 180s the Han emperors were puppets of palace eunuchs, and famine and plague stalked the land. In 184 hundreds of thousands of farmers rose under a faith healer, Zhang Jue, wearing yellow headscarves. The generals who crushed the Yellow Turbans became warlords with armies of their own.

The strongest of them, Cao Cao, took the young emperor under his protection in 196 and ruled northern China in his name. A fine poet and a ruthless general, he was later cast as the great villain of the story.

In 208 Cao Cao sailed down the Yangtze with a huge fleet to finish off his rivals in the south. Sun Quan and Liu Bei joined against him. At Red Cliffs their general Zhou Yu sent burning ships into his fleet, and with sickness in his camp, Cao Cao turned back north. China would stay divided.

In 220 Cao Cao's son made the last Han emperor give up the throne and founded Wei in the north. Liu Bei, who claimed Han royal blood, made himself emperor of Shu in the southwest, and Sun Quan in time of Wu in the southeast. Three rulers each claimed to be the only Son of Heaven.

Liu Bei's chief minister, Zhuge Liang, nicknamed the Sleeping Dragon, became China's model of the wise strategist. After Liu Bei died he led five campaigns north across the mountains against Wei, and died in camp in 234, still fighting.

In the novel, Zhuge Liang must find 100,000 arrows in three days. He sends boats lined with straw dummies toward Cao Cao's camp in thick fog, with drums beating. Cao Cao's archers shoot into the fog, and the boats come back bristling with arrows. It never happened, but every Chinese child knows it.

Wars, famine and plague emptied the country. A Han census of 157 counted 56 million people; the count of 280 found only 16 million. Many had fled or slipped out of the records, but the loss of life was still enormous.

In the end none of the three kingdoms won. Wei conquered Shu in 263. Then a Wei general's grandson, Sima Yan, took the throne for his own family, the Jin, and in 280 conquered Wu. China was one again, though not for long.

In the 1300s Luo Guanzhong turned the history into a long novel of loyalty and cunning, which opens with Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei swearing brotherhood in a peach garden. It is still retold in operas, comics, TV series and video games.

The Three Kingdoms lasted barely sixty years but became the best loved story of Chinese history. Its heroes are everywhere in East Asia: Guan Yu, Liu Bei's sworn brother, is worshipped as a god of loyalty in temples, shops and police stations.
